title: Python Basics
description: Core Python 3.13 concepts, from print() to functions.

steps.title: Why Python?
steps.body:
Python is a **high-level** language famous for clear, readable code. It powers **web apps**, **data science**, **automation** and **AI**.

In this course you will learn the core ideas every Python program is built from.

steps.title: Interpreted and Interactive
steps.body:
Python is an **interpreted** language: your code runs line by line with no separate compile step, so experiments are fast.

You can type code at an **interactive prompt** or save it in a **script** and run it whenever you like.

steps.title: Your first program
steps.code:
print("Hello, Python!")
name = "Ada"
print("Nice to meet you,", name)

notes.text: print() shows text on the screen.
A variable named name now stores the string "Ada".
print() accepts several values and separates them with a space.

steps.output:
Hello, Python!
Nice to meet you, Ada

steps.title: Python as a calculator
steps.code:
# Python as a calculator
print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)
print(10 / 4)
print(10 // 4)

notes.text: Multiplication happens before addition, so this is 2 + 12.
Parentheses change the order of evaluation.
A single slash always gives a float result.
Double slash is floor division and drops the fraction.

steps.question: What does print(7 // 2) display?
steps.explanation: Floor division rounds the result down to a whole number, so 7 // 2 is 3.

steps.question: Which statement about Python is true?
options: Python needs a separate compile step before every run
Python can only be used for websites
steps.explanation: Python uses indentation to group statements into blocks.

steps.title: Interactive mode and scripts
steps.body:
Start the interpreter by typing **python3**. It shows the **>>>** prompt and evaluates each line you type.

For larger programs, save code in a file such as **app.py** and run it with **python3 app.py**.

steps.title: Comments and quotes
steps.body:
A **#** starts a comment that Python ignores. Strings can use **single** or **double** quotes, so you can write 'it is' or "it's" without trouble.

Good comments explain **why** the code exists, not what each line already says.

steps.title: Comments in action
steps.code:
# This is a comment
text = "Python"  # trailing comment
print(text)
print(len(text))

notes.text: The whole line is ignored by Python.
A comment can follow code on the same line.
len() counts the characters in a string.

steps.title: Meeting the sys module
steps.code:
import sys
print(sys.version_info.major)
print(__name__)

notes.text: import loads a module from the standard library.
version_info.major is the major Python version number.
When run as a script, __name__ equals "__main__".

steps.question: Which symbol starts a comment in Python?
steps.explanation: Python comments begin with the # character.

steps.question: What prompt does the interactive interpreter show?
What does this script print?
steps.code:
x = 5
x + 1
print(x)
steps.explanation: In a script, the bare expression x + 1 is evaluated but not printed. Only print(x) outputs 5.

steps.title: Numbers
steps.body: Python has **int** for whole numbers and **float** for decimals. Use **+ - * /** as expected, **//** for floor division, **%** for remainder and **\*\*** for powers.

steps.title: Strings
steps.body:
A **string** is text in quotes. You can **index** characters with square brackets, **slice** ranges with a colon, and join strings with **+**.

**f-strings** let you embed values: f"Hi {name}".

steps.title: Number operators
steps.code:
a = 17
b = 5
print(a / b)
print(a // b)
print(a % b)
print(a ** 2)

notes.text: True division gives 3.4.
Floor division gives 3.
The remainder of 17 divided by 5 is 2.
Two stars raise to a power: 17 squared.

steps.title: Indexing and slicing
steps.code:
word = "Python"
print(word[0])
print(word[-1])
print(word[0:2])
print(word + "!" * 3)

notes.text: Index 0 is the first character.
Negative indexes count from the end.
A slice stops before the end index.
Repetition happens before concatenation.

steps.title: f-strings
steps.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
print(f"{3.14159:.2f}")

notes.text: Curly braces insert variable values into the string.
The :.2f format rounds to two decimal places.

steps.question: What does this print?
steps.code:
word = "Python"
print(word[1:4])
steps.explanation: A slice from index 1 up to (not including) 4 gives yth.

steps.title: Lists hold sequences
steps.body:
A **list** stores items in order, written with square brackets: [1, 2, 3]. Lists can hold **any** type and even mix types.

Items are reached by **index**, starting at 0.

steps.title: Lists are mutable
steps.body:
Lists can be **changed** after creation. Useful methods include **append()**, **pop()**, **sort()** and **insert()**.

Built-ins such as **len()**, **sum()** and **max()** work on lists too.

steps.title: Building a list
steps.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("date")
print(fruits)
print(fruits[1])
print(len(fruits))

notes.text: append adds an item to the end.
Printing a list shows its brackets and quotes.
Index 1 is the second item.
len counts the items.

steps.title: Sorting and slicing
steps.code:
nums = [5, 2, 9, 1]
nums.sort()
print(nums)
print(nums[1:3])
print(sum(nums))
print(max(nums))

notes.text: sort() reorders the list in place.
A slice returns a new list.
sum adds all the numbers.
max finds the largest item.

steps.title: List comprehensions
steps.code:
squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)

notes.text: A comprehension builds a new list from a loop in one line.
range(1, 6) produced 1 through 5.

steps.question: What does this print?
steps.code:
lst = [1, 2, 3]
lst.append(4)
print(lst[-1])
steps.explanation: After append(4) the last item, index -1, is 4.

steps.question: Which method removes and returns the last item of a list?
steps.explanation: pop() with no argument removes and returns the last item.

steps.title: Making decisions
steps.body: **if**, **elif** and **else** choose which block runs. Conditions use comparison operators like **==**, **!=**, **<** and **>**, and can be combined with **and**, **or** and **not**.

steps.title: Repeating work
steps.body:
A **for** loop walks over a sequence, and **range()** generates numbers. A **while** loop repeats while a condition stays true.

Use **break** to leave a loop and **continue** to skip to the next round.

steps.title: if / elif / else

notes.text: False, because 25 is not above 30.
True, so this branch runs.
Skipped because an earlier branch matched.

steps.title: for loops

notes.text: range(3) yields 0, 1 and 2.
+= adds to the variable in place.
This line is outside the loop, so it runs once.

steps.title: while and break

notes.text: while True would run forever without a break.
break leaves the loop immediately.

steps.question: Which numbers does range(2, 5) produce?
steps.explanation: range stops before the end value.

steps.question: What does this print?
steps.explanation: When i is 2 the loop continues without printing.

steps.title: Defining functions
steps.body:
A function packages reusable code. Use **def**, a name, parameters in parentheses and an indented body. **return** sends a value back to the caller.

A function without return gives back **None**.

steps.title: Parameters and scope
steps.body:
Parameters can have **default values** and be passed by **keyword**. Variables created inside a function are **local** and disappear when it ends.

***args** collects any number of extra positional values.

steps.title: A simple function
steps.code:
def square(x):
    return x * x

print(square(4))
print(square(square(2)))

notes.text: def starts the definition and x is a parameter.
return hands the answer back.
Calls the function with 4.
Function calls can be nested.

steps.title: Defaults and keywords
steps.code:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}!"

print(greet("Ada"))
print(greet("Linus", greeting="Hi"))

notes.text: greeting has a default value.
Uses the default greeting.
A keyword argument overrides the default.

steps.title: Variable arguments

notes.text: *numbers collects all positional arguments in a tuple.
With no arguments the tuple is empty, so the sum is 0.

steps.question: What does a function without a return statement give back?
steps.explanation: Functions without return give back None.

steps.question: What does this print?
steps.explanation: y defaults to 2, so f(3) is 3 * 2.
